body.heading: The routine
paragraphs: Take a four-digit number whose digits are not all the same — say 3524. Arrange the digits to make the largest number (5432) and the smallest (2345) and subtract: 5432 − 2345 = 3087. Repeat: 8730 − 0378 = 8352. Again: 8532 − 2358 = 6174.

Now try to leave. 7641 − 1467 = 6174. The number is a trapdoor: once you land on it, the routine maps it to itself forever. The Indian mathematician D. R. Kaprekar described this in 1949, and 6174 is called Kaprekar's constant.

body.heading: Every road leads there
paragraphs: The startling part is that 6174 is not just an example — every four-digit number with at least two different digits reaches it, in at most seven rounds of the routine. Mathematicians have checked them all; there are no exceptions and no escape routes.
Three-digit numbers have their own trapdoor: 495. Try 321: 321 − 123 = 198; 981 − 189 = 792; 972 − 279 = 693; 963 − 369 = 594; 954 − 459 = 495 — and there it stays.

body.heading: Try it: race to the constant
paragraphs: Each player picks a secret four-digit number, then everyone performs the routine on their own number, counting the steps. Compare: who took the longest road to 6174? (Seven steps is the maximum — see if anyone's number achieves it.)

Then investigate like a mathematician: what goes wrong with a number like 1111, whose digits are all the same? The routine collapses to zero, which is why the rule insists on at least two different digits.

takeaway: Kaprekar's routine is a funnel in number space: thousands of starting points, one resting place — 6174.
